Practice

Good design starts with the problem, not the solution. Everything else follows from there.

Before I open a design tool, I want to understand what we are actually trying to solve, who it affects, and why it matters. That means asking questions that don't have easy answers, sitting with ambiguity longer than feels comfortable, and resisting the pull toward solutions before the problem is clear.

I work best as a collaborator. Design doesn't happen in isolation, and the outcomes I'm most proud of came from thinking out loud alongside engineers, researchers, and stakeholders who genuinely cared about getting it right. I push back when something doesn't add up. I bring people in early. I try to make the process feel less like a handoff and more like a shared effort.

Being a generalist means I can hold the whole picture at once. I move between systems thinking and pixel-level decisions, between brand strategy and front-end code, between research findings and interface details. That range isn't about doing everything. It's about seeing how each piece connects to the rest, and making sure the small decisions serve the larger ones.

I care a lot about craft. Not for its own sake, but because the details signal to the people using something whether it was made with care or without it. Sloppy motion, inconsistent spacing, a label that doesn't quite say the right thing. These things accumulate. Getting them right is part of the work.

I start iterating quickly and refine over time. Rough ideas shared early beat polished work shared late. Feedback is easier to absorb before you're attached. The best version of anything I've ever made went through a lot of versions that weren't good yet.

AI in Practice

I've been integrating AI into how I work.

Cursor for writing and debugging code, Claude for reasoning through design problems, Figma Make for rapid prototyping and concept work. The honest answer is: it has changed how fast I can move. A design system that used to take weeks now takes a day. A site that would have taken a month took a week. That acceleration is real and I find it valuable.

I'm still working out where I stand on it. The energy cost of running large models at scale is real and underreported. The effect on design as a profession, on junior practitioners especially, is something I think about. I don't have a clean answer. What I know is that I'd rather be honest about using it, critical of its limitations, and thoughtful about when it helps and when it flattens the work.

Below are a few things I've made with AI recently. Not a portfolio, more of a running log of what's working and what I'm learning.

Design System in a Day

Token architecture, component library, and documentation built in hours. Used Claude to reason through naming conventions and Cursor to scaffold the code. What used to take weeks compressed into a single focused session.

This Site

Built and iterated on jamesmadson.me with Claude handling the heavy lifting on SCSS architecture, accessibility improvements, and debugging. I focused on design decisions. It shipped faster and cleaner than anything I've hand-coded solo.

Nonprofit Usability Audit

Used AI-assisted code review and heuristic analysis to debug and improve usability on a site I volunteer with. Identified issues I'd walked past a hundred times, fixed them in an afternoon.

Brand Guidelines to Brand Site

Took a static PDF brand guidelines document and transformed it into a living brand site. AI handled the structural translation and component scaffolding while I shaped the experience and editorial voice.

AI Brand Skill

Built a prompt-based brand skill that teams can add to their AI system of choice. It lets people design and write on-brand copy for prototypes, decks, and video scripts without needing to reinterpret the guidelines every time.
